newsitem.title: ITALY: Zaire crisis casts shadow on food summit.
newsitem.headline: Zaire crisis casts shadow on food summit.

text.p: The crisis in Zaire overshadowed the opening of the World Food Summit on Wednesday as U.N. Secretary General Boutros Boutros-Ghali urged action to help a sea of refugees wandering "helpless in the mountains and forests."

Boutros-Ghali's vivid description of the plight of starving Hutu refugees caught in ethnic fighting brought home the urgency of the summit's goal: to find ways of reducing drastically the number of hungry people in the world.
"It is this terrible reality which we must keep in mind to understand how and why we have to act," Boutros-Ghali said.
He told delegates from 194 countries that only with a "collective, concerted" effort could the tragedy of the Great Lakes region of Africa be resolved.

"At the very moment this summit is taking place, over a million starving, frightened refugees are wandering helpless in the mountains and forests of eastern Zaire," he told the opening session of the five-day summit.
"For the tribes and ethnic groups who are killing each other hunger and famine are, in the final analysis, weapons of war to be used to kill and kill again," he said.
The leader of Zaire's delegation to the summit, Deputy Prime Minister Mutombo Bakafwa Nsenda, was reluctant to talk about the situation in his country.
But he told a Reuters reporter that Boutros-Ghali's plea for action "risks coming a bit late."
In an unveiled bid to win support for a multinational force to be sent to Zaire to bring food and secure safe passage for the refugees, Boutros-Ghali said:
"From this platform, in this Eternal City, I make a solemn appeal to peoples and to states to take part, all of them, in the collective action we will undertake in the Great Lakes region".

The U.N. chief confirmed on Tuesday that Canada had offered to lead the multinational force. He said he expected the U.N. Security Council to approve a mandate in a few days and was returning to New York later on Wednesday.
The crisis in eastern Zaire, where Hutu refugees from past ethnic slaughter in Rwanda and Burundi have been put to flight by fresh violence, is not officially on the summit's agenda.
But it was foremost in informal discussions on the margins of the meetings and in comments by delegates to the media.
Tanzanian President Benjamin William Mkapa told Reuters in an interview that he hoped groups would stop their fighting to allow help to reach the refugees.

"My hope is that those who are combatting each other now... will respect the very noble and humanitarian mission of such a neutral force which seeks to secure the sanctuaries and the corridors," Mkapa said.
He spoke shortly after the United Nations halted efforts to distribute a first consignment of aid in eastern Zaire when four shells slammed into a hill in the city of Goma.
Mkapa urged the international community to move more quickly and called for refugees to return to their homes.
"The immediate question...is accessibility of relief assistance in order to preserve the lives of those wandering refugees there," he said.

"Subsequent to that I hope we shall move at record speed in order to secure the rapid repatriation of refugees...because in the last analysis that may have been the real springboard of this chaos that has happened."
